### Overview The Alert for Price Spikes (ALPS) dataset tracks the current prices of key staple food commodities and compares them to expected prices, which are calculated based on seasonal trends. An ALPS value is assigned to a given commodity at a particular market based on how much its current price differs from the expected price. This value is used to categorize a commodity’s price into one of four categories: normal, stress, alert, or crisis. Food prices on a local market often correlated with food security crises. Food price spikes can have devastating impacts for rural households in developing countries since they spend a large percentage of income on food. ALPS serves three main purposes for decision-making. First, it can serve as a price monitoring tool that allows users to identify price abnormalities. Second, ALPS can generate early warning information that enables users to prepare and act to reduce harm to households most vulnerable to food price fluctuations. Third, ALPS can trigger contingency planning by anticipating food price crises. The ALPS dataset is generated by the World Food Programme (WFP) and monitors markets spanning more than 60 countries. The time period over which prices have been tracked varies by location, but certain markets have food price data as early as 1994. The data is updated monthly for markets that are actively being monitored. ### Methodology Seasonal price trends were determined through reference to monthly commodity prices recorded in the WFP's Vulnerability Analysis and Mapping (VAM) Food and Commodity Price dataset. This dataset was collected by WFP country offices, national government agencies, and partner organizations. The ALPS indicator level was calculated in four steps: - **Estimation of seasonal price trends**: The seasonal price trend was calculated using a linear regression of market price data over the entire period for which data was available. Both the long-term trend and monthly fluctuations, related to the production or demand of a commodity, were included in the regression. - **Calculation of the difference between market price and estimated price**: The difference between the observed price and the expected price based on seasonal trends was calculated for each month. - **Calculation of the ALPS indicator considering price volatility**: Each month’s difference was divided by the standard deviation of the differences over all of the recorded months, producing the value of the ALPS indicator. - **Categorization of the ALPS indicator**: Based on the ALPS indicator value, markets were assigned to one of four situations: (1) Normal: ALPS < 0.25; (2) Stress: 0.25 ≤ ALPS < 1; (3) Alert: 1 ≤ ALPS < 2; (4) Crisis: ALPS ≥ 2. ### Overview This dataset shows forecasted fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations at Earth’s surface, modeled by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Goddard Earth Observing System Composition Forecast (GEOS-CF). PM2.5 is an air pollutant made up of fine inhalable particles, with diameters of 2.5 micrometers and smaller. These particles come in many shapes and can be made up of hundreds of different chemicals. Some are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites, unpaved roads, fields, smokestacks, or fires. Most particles form in the atmosphere as a result of complex reactions of chemicals such as sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which are pollutants emitted from power plants and automobiles. The size of these particles allows them to get deep into your lungs, and some may even get into your bloodstream. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution/health-and-environmental-effects-particulate-matter-pm), exposure to such particles can affect both your lungs and your heart. Numerous scientific studies have linked particle pollution exposure to a variety of problems, including premature death in people with heart or lung disease, heart attacks, irregular heartbeat, aggravated asthma, decreased lung function, increased respiratory symptoms, such as irritation of the airways, coughing, or difficulty breathing. People with heart or lung diseases, children, and older adults are the most likely to be affected by fine particulate exposure. Resource Watch also shows GEOS-CF forecasts for [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ebc079a1-51d8-4622-ba25-d8f3b4fcf8b3) and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ecce902d-a322-4d13-a3d6-e1a36fc5573e). The GEOS-CF system runs once a day and produces a global, near-real-time forecast up to five days into the future at 15-minute and one-hour time intervals. The data has a global coverage at a resolution of 25 kilometers x 25 kilometers. GEOS-CF also creates global forecasts for a variety of other air quality indicators. GEOS-CF was developed by NASA's Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO). You can find forecasted concentrations for each compound on the GMAO website. ### Methodology The GEOS-CF model provides analysis on the composition of a range of air pollutants including PM2.5, O₃, and NO₂. This model is driven by the GEOS weather forecasting system and the GEOS-Chem atmospheric chemistry model. To produce estimates of aerosol concentrations, the GEOS-CF model runs two aerosol schemes: the GEOS-Chem aerosol mechanism (GCC) and the Goddard Chemistry, Aerosol, Radiation, and Transport (GOCART) module to simulate the effects of aerosols in the atmosphere. The GOCART aerosols are constrained by satellite observed aerosol optical depth, while the GCC aerosols are purely model derived. The PM2.5 data shown on Resource Watch is produced by the GOCART module. All emissions modeling for GEOS-Chem is handled by the [NASA-Harvard emissions component (HEMCO)](https://www.geosci-model-dev.net/7/1409/2014/gmd-7-1409-2014.html), a stand-alone software component for calculating emissions in global atmospheric models. Anthropogenic emissions are acquired as monthly averages from the [HTAPv2.2](https://www.atmos-chem-phys.net/15/11411/2015/) and [RETRO](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1029/2007GB003031) emissions inventories. The monthly averages are broken down into hourly values by sector-specific factors. Emissions of CO ([Oda et al., 2017](https://www.earth-syst-sci-data.net/10/87/2018/)) and SO₂ ([Liu et al., 2018](https://www.atmos-chem-phys.net/18/16571/2018/)) are scaled using a factor based on satellite data. Emissions from biomass burning are taken from [Quick Fire Emissions Database (QFEDv2.5)](https://gmao.gsfc.nasa.gov/pubs/docs/Darmenov796.pdf), volcanic emissions of SO₂ are from [CARN (2019)](https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/MSVOLSO2L4_3/summary), and other natural emissions are taken from various sources. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://gmao.gsfc.nasa.gov/pubs/docs/Knowland1159.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows GEOS-CF forecasts for [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ebc079a1-51d8-4622-ba25-d8f3b4fcf8b3) and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ecce902d-a322-4d13-a3d6-e1a36fc5573e). This dataset, created by the Global Land Analysis and Discovery (GLAD) lab at the University of Maryland and supported by Global Forest Watch, is the first Landsat-based alert system for tree cover loss. While most existing loss alert products use 250 m resolution MODIS imagery, these alerts have a 30 m resolution and thus can detect loss at a much finer spatial scale. The alerts are currently operational in the tropics. New Landsat 7 and 8 images are downloaded as they are posted online at USGS EROS, assessed for cloud cover or poor data quality, and compared to the 4 previous years of Landsat-derived metrics (including ranks, means, and regressions of red, near infrared, and shortwave infrared bands, and ranks of NDVI, NBR, and NDWI). The metrics and the latest Landsat image are run through decision trees to calculate a median probability of forest disturbance. Pixels with probability > 50% are reported as tree cover loss alerts. For more information on methodology, see the paper in Environmental Research Letters. Alerts remain unconfirmed until 2 or more loss observations occur out of 4 observations or within 180 days. ### Overview The Air Quality: Mexico City Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Forecast dataset provides weather and air quality forecasts for Mexico City. This dataset represents the forecasted density of fine particulate matter in micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3). The forecast offers an hourly estimate on fine particulate matter density with a spatial resolution of 1 kilometer (km), encompassing Mexico CIty and its Metropolitan Area (MCMA). PM2.5 are fine inhalable particles, with diameters that are generally 2.5 micrometers and smaller. These particles come in many sizes and shapes and can be made up of hundreds of different chemicals. Some are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites or smokestacks, while others are created from complex reactions in the atmosphere. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)](https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution/particulate-matter-pm-basics) the size of these particles allows them to get deep into the lungs, and some may even go into the bloodstream. Some of the health problems related to the exposure to PM2.5 include: premature death in people with heart or lung disease, nonfatal heart attacks, irregular heartbeat, aggravated asthma, decreased lung function, and increased respiratory symptoms. People with heart or lung diseases, children, and older adults are most likely to be affected by particle pollution exposure. According to the [Mexico City Ministry of the Environment (SEDEMA)]((http://www.aire.cdmx.gob.mx/descargas/publicaciones/flippingbook/informe_anual_calidad_aire_2017/mobile/informe_anual_calidad_aire_2017v3.pdf), PM2.5 emissions in the MCMA frequently exceed the limits established byMexican regulations, as well as the standards of the World Health Organization (WHO) and the EPA. The city's suburbs tend to have the highest levels of this pollutant, which is associated with the industrial activity in the area. Showcasing the spatial distribution of PM2.5 in the MCMA will provide insight about the way a city can produce information according to its needs while complementing global air quality models. The forecast helps the Mexico CIty government to issue health warnings based on the expected air quality for a given day, like recommending citizens to avoid open-air exercise or to limit their use of fossil fuel vehicles. The forecast was generated by the SEDEMA with help from the Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC). SEDEMA provides a tool for the inhabitants of MCMA to make well-informed decisions about dangerous air pollution activity on a given day. SEDEMA works on five environmental issues: air quality and climate change, land conservation and biodiversity, sustainable urban infrastructure, water supply and quality, and environmental communication and education. ### Methodology The dataset is comprised of the following models: Weather: Estimates the weather conditions of the MCMA using data from global systems. It harnesses the [Weather Research and Forecasting Model-Advanced Research (WRF-ARW)](https://www.mmm.ucar.edu/weather-research-and-forecasting-model), which is a mesoscale numerical weather prediction system designed for both atmospheric research and operational forecasting applications. The model generates temperature, wind, rainfall and solar radiation, among other weather related indicators.among others. Emissions: This model makes use of emission inventories for the MCMA to estimate PM2.5 levels on an hourly basis, as well as its geospatial distribution. Chemical Transport: This model harnesses the outputs from the weather and emissions models as well as other chemical and physical mechanisms to simulate transformations in the atmosphere and the influence of weather dynamics in these processes. For this purpose, the [Community Multiscale Air Quality Modeling System (CMAQ)] (https://www.cmascenter.org/cmaq/) is employed to forecast the behavior of the pollutants in the MCMA. ### Overview The Conflict Forecast dataset categorizes areas by their modeled risk of conflict over the following 12 months. Each district is labeled with one of the following: emerging conflict, ongoing conflict, or peace. Conflict is defined by the subnational administrative district (ADM-2), forecasted to have at least 10 fatalities in the next 12 months using a random forest machine model that learns from past records and optimizes its predictive power. The forecast incorporates frequently updated environmental variables, including water indicators, in order to capture the many stressors that may lead to conflict. Updated forecasts are released on a quarterly basis. This forecast was produced by researchers at the World Resources Institute (WRI) and the Hague Center for Strategic Studies (HCSS) under the Water, Peace, and Security Partnership (WPS). ### Methodology This model forecasts conflict up to a year in advance using a random forest machine learning model. It was measured with the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) data over a 12-month period. Conflict is defined as organized violence resulting in at least 10 fatalities. Machine learning techniques are adept at detecting subtle or complex patterns within large volumes of data without requiring a priori instructions or a theoretical framework. Since conflict literature does not offer a clear consensus on what factors contribute to violence, nor on the causal pathways to conflict, machine learning was identified as a viable means of establishing quantitative linkages between local conditions and the subsequent emergence (or continuation, or cessation) of conflict. The data used as indicators in the model capture a wide range of factors—from socioeconomics to governance to biophysical phenomena—and are correspondingly collected at a variety of geographic and temporal resolutions. In order to utilize and analyze them in concert, data was reconciled to a common unit of analysis: the ADM-2 month. Only districts with at least three years of recorded organized violence within the selected conflict database were eligible for inclusion in the modeling process. Currently, the geographic scope is limited to the following regions: Africa, Asia, and the Middle East. The model used historical data to learn to “predict” past conflict outcomes based on past conditions. The model was then applied to a separate tranche of more recent historical data and used its performance on this validation data to estimate the model’s predictive power on “true” forecasts made based on current conditions. When applied to test data, the model captures 86 percent of future conflicts. The model’s conflict signal is noisy, with half of conflict predictions representing false positives. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset.
